name: Efpeglenatide
evidenceNote: A phase 3 program of several large randomized trials, including a 4,076-person cardiovascular outcomes trial, plus a Korean phase 3 obesity trial. No US application has been announced.
summary: Efpeglenatide is a weekly GLP-1 drug that cut heart events 27% in a 4,076-person trial. It is unapproved in the US but was approved in South Korea in 2026.
keyTakeaway: Efpeglenatide is a once-weekly GLP-1 receptor agonist from Hanmi Pharmaceutical, built from an exendin-4 peptide joined to an antibody fragment. In the AMPLITUDE-O trial of 4,076 people with type 2 diabetes and heart or kidney disease, it lowered major cardiovascular events by 27% versus placebo. Sanofi, then its partner, ended funding for the wider diabetes program, and no FDA filing followed. In October 2026, South Korea approved it for weight management as Eppe after a local trial showed 9% weight loss at 40 weeks. It is not FDA-approved.

atGlance.label: FDA status
atGlance.value: Not approved or filed in the US; approved in South Korea for weight management (2026)

atGlance.label: How it works
atGlance.value: Activates GLP-1 receptors; an attached antibody fragment slows clearance for weekly dosing

atGlance.label: Research
atGlance.value: Large phase 3 trials in type 2 diabetes, including a positive cardiovascular outcomes trial

blocks.text: Efpeglenatide is a GLP-1 receptor agonist developed by the Korean company Hanmi Pharmaceutical under the code HM11260C. Most approved GLP-1 drugs, such as semaglutide, are modeled on human GLP-1. Efpeglenatide is instead based on exendin-4, a related peptide that also activates the GLP-1 receptor [1][5].

To make it last, the exendin-4 analog is chemically linked through a short polyethylene glycol spacer to the Fc fragment, the stem portion, of a human IgG4 antibody. Hanmi calls this platform LAPSCOVERY [5]. The result is a large molecule that circulates for days, designed for weekly or potentially less frequent injection.

items.text: The Sanofi-funded AMPLITUDE-O outcomes trial is published in the New England Journal of Medicine [1].
A phase 1b study finds weekly efpeglenatide slows stomach emptying about as much as daily liraglutide [7].
Three other AMPLITUDE glycemic trials are reported; all were ended early by the sponsor because of funding, not safety or efficacy [4].
South Korea's Ministry of Food and Drug Safety approves efpeglenatide for chronic weight management as Eppe [6].

blocks.text: Efpeglenatide binds the GLP-1 receptor, the target shared by every drug in the class, which lowers blood sugar and body weight. In a randomized phase 1b study, weekly efpeglenatide delayed stomach emptying about as much as daily liraglutide and improved the insulin-producing beta cells' response to glucose [7]. Few people in its monotherapy trial had low blood sugar, consistent with the glucose-dependent way GLP-1 drugs raise insulin [3].

The antibody fragment is what sets it apart. Fc-containing proteins are recycled by a receptor called FcRn rather than broken down quickly, which keeps them in circulation. A 2025 pooled analysis of six studies estimated a very low clearance for efpeglenatide, similar to dulaglutide, another Fc-fused GLP-1 drug, and found exposure rose roughly in proportion to dose with weekly injection [5].

No. No FDA application for efpeglenatide has been announced. Its global diabetes program, funded by Sanofi, produced a positive outcomes trial [1], but three of its phase 3 glycemic trials were stopped early by the sponsor for funding reasons [4], and development since has been led by Hanmi with a focus on obesity [5].

Outside the United States, South Korea approved efpeglenatide in October 2026 for chronic weight management in adults without diabetes who have obesity, or overweight plus a weight-related condition. It is sold there as a weekly auto-injector under the name Eppe [6]. That approval does not make it legally available in the US.

Efpeglenatide has more randomized human data behind it than most unapproved peptides. The headline result is AMPLITUDE-O, run at 344 sites in 28 countries in people with type 2 diabetes plus either heart disease or reduced kidney function and another risk factor [1].

rows: 4,076 adults with type 2 diabetes and heart or kidney disease, median 1.8 years
Major cardiovascular events 7.0% vs 9.2% (hazard ratio 0.73); kidney composite 13.0% vs 18.4%
618 participants also taking an SGLT2 inhibitor
Benefit did not differ by SGLT2 inhibitor use
Type 2 diabetes on diet and exercise, 30 weeks
HbA1c down 0.5% to 1.0% more than placebo, depending on dose
Non-inferior to dulaglutide 1.5 mg on HbA1c; about 3 kg weight loss in all groups

blocks.text: Digestive effects were the main side effects. In AMPLITUDE-O, diarrhea, constipation, nausea, vomiting, and bloating were all more common on efpeglenatide than on placebo [1]. In the Korean obesity trial, diarrhea affected 17.6% and nausea 16.6% of treated participants [6].

Two caveats apply. The Korean obesity results were reported at a 40-week interim point, and the final 64-week average had not been disclosed when the drug was approved [6]. The weight loss is also smaller than reported for approved weight drugs such as Wegovy and Mounjaro, though trial populations and designs differ [6].

sections.heading: How is efpeglenatide different from semaglutide?

blocks.text: Both are weekly injections that act on the same receptor, but they are built differently. Semaglutide is a modified human GLP-1 that shares 94% of the natural sequence and lasts about a week by binding albumin in the blood [8]. Efpeglenatide starts from exendin-4 and gets its long life from an attached antibody fragment, which makes it a far larger molecule that is cleared through the same recycling route as antibodies [5].

Their evidence also sits in different places. Semaglutide has outcome trials in diabetes, obesity, heart disease, and kidney disease, and holds FDA approval [8]. Efpeglenatide's outcomes trial, AMPLITUDE-O, enrolled a high-risk diabetes population and also cut a combined kidney endpoint (falling kidney function or heavy protein in the urine) from 18.4% to 13.0% of participants [1]. No head-to-head trial has compared the two drugs.
